title: LD-MoLE: Learnable Dynamic Routing for Mixture of LoRA Experts
one_liner: Instead of deciding upfront how many expert adapters to activate per token, learn a separate small network that predicts the right number for each token, token by token, at each layer.
lead: Large language models are too big to retrain efficiently. LoRA is a trick: instead of retraining millions of weights, you train tiny adapters on the side, one per task. A newer idea: mixture of LoRA experts, which trains multiple adapters and routes each token to the best ones. But today's routers use TopK: pick the top K adapters by score. The problem: you have to decide K upfront, and K is the same for every token and every layer. LD-MoLE fixes this. It learns a separate tiny network that predicts the exact number of adapters to use for each token at each layer—some tokens get 2, others get 8—and does it all in a way that lets the whole model learn end-to-end.

problem.h2: Today's routers freeze the expert count upfront
paras: Imagine fine-tuning a large language model. You do not retrain all its weights—that costs too much. Instead, you add tiny trainable adapters (LoRA modules, each a small network bolted onto the side). A single adapter is weak, so you train many of them. Now each token arriving at a layer must pick which adapters to use. Old idea: hardcode a selector that always picks the top K. Pipe the token's embedding (a list of numbers representing that token) through a scoring function, rank the experts by score, and take the K with the highest scores. This works, but K is a knob: you guess how many experts each token needs, set K to the same number everywhere, and hope it fits all tokens and all layers equally. If K is too big, you waste computation on useless experts. If K is too small, tokens lack what they need.

callout.html: TopK routers treat every token and every layer the same: same number of experts chosen, no adaptation.

steps.text: A token's embedding arrives at a LoRA-mixture layer.
A shared tiny MLP predicts how many adapters this token needs right now.
The router scores each adapter. It converts those scores into smooth weights (each weight between 0 and 1, all adding to 1).
Take the top K by score. Send the token through those K adapters in parallel.
Combine the adapter outputs using their smooth weights as multipliers.

object.h2: What the paper moves: the expert count per token
paras: The paper changes the expert count from a fixed knob to a learned, token-specific number. Instead of always picking the top 8 adapters, the method learns to pick the top 3 for simple tokens and the top 8 for complex ones. This learned count changes from layer to layer and token to token. The routing now has one extra tiny network: a shared MLP that predicts a sparsity factor (a threshold number) for each token. That threshold determines how many experts route to this token right now.

hidden.h2: The sparsity factor: controlling how many experts activate
hidden.name: sparsity factor (lambda)
paras: The sparsity factor is a single number per token that controls the expert threshold. The paper predicts it with a tiny shared MLP given the token's embedding. Higher sparsity factor means more experts pass the threshold and activate; lower means fewer. The paper learns to set this factor differently for each token, each layer. It measures how many experts end up activated by counting, and adds a loss term that steers the sparsity factor toward values that give the target sparsity level (for example, activate exactly 4 experts when you want that target).

heat.caption: Darker cells mean higher sparsity factor (more experts activate). Each cell is one token at one layer.

reads.html: The sparsity factor is a per-token number that a tiny network predicts. Higher sparsity factor means more adapters activate for that token.
The sparsity factor lambda is predicted by a lightweight shared MLP and governs the projection function that determines which experts route to each token, derived from closed-form optimization.

mechanism.h2: Why learning the expert count fixes the problem
paras: The paper solves TopK's rigidity by treating expert selection as a smooth optimization problem. Instead of a hard cutoff (pick exactly K), it uses a soft projection that turns scores into probabilities, and derives a closed-form solution that tells you exactly which experts to pick. This closed-form solution depends on a single threshold number: the sparsity factor. The paper then trains a tiny shared MLP to predict the sparsity factor for each token. Because the factor is just a number, the MLP trains end-to-end with gradient steps (small nudges to the MLP weights based on whether it predicted the right factor for that token). The model learns which factor value works best for each token at each layer. Tokens that need many experts get a high factor; tokens that need few get a low factor. This adaptation happens during training, learned from data, not guessed upfront.

The paper also adds a sparsity loss that steers the sparsity factor toward target values. If you want each token to use roughly 4 experts on average, the loss gently pushes the factor to values that produce that count. This stabilizes training and prevents collapse (a common failure where all tokens route to the same one or two experts).

stages.s: Shared MLP predicts sparsity factor for this token
Router scores each expert, applies differentiable projection
Experts with high enough score activate
Sparsity loss corrects factor if count drifts from target
Token routed to learned number of experts

math.h2: The routing equation with learned sparsity
math.words: The router computes a score for each expert, then applies a smooth projection that depends on a sparsity threshold. The projection selects experts whose scores are above the threshold. The threshold is predicted by a small MLP from the token embedding. The loss term steers the threshold toward values that produce the target number of selected experts.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Token 1 arrives. Its embedding has dimension 768.
MLP_lambda predicts lambda is 0.6 for this token (sparsity factor).
Projection with lambda 0.6: experts with score at least 0.6 activate. Experts 1, 2, 3 pass threshold.
num_active is 3. Target k is 4. Loss sees mismatch, nudges lambda up on next update.
Token 2 arrives. MLP predicts lambda is 0.3 for this token (different embedding).
Expert scores: [0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1]. Projection: 5 experts pass (scores at least 0.3).
MLP learned: simple tokens get low lambda (2-3 experts), complex tokens get high lambda (6-8 experts).

math.note: The sparsity factor lambda is learned per-token per-layer, so the same token uses different numbers of experts at different layers.

charts.title: Fixed TopK (old way)
charts.note: All tokens use 8 adapters, even if only 2 are enough. Adapters trained on wrong mix.

charts.title: Learned dynamic routing (LD-MoLE)
charts.note: Simple tokens use 2 experts, complex use 8. Routing matches the task. All tokens improve because each token now routes to the right number of experts for its needs, not wasting compute on unnecessary adapters or starving on too few.

items.html: If the sparsity loss is too weak, all tokens learn to route to the same expert, wasting the mixture. The paper adds a load-balancing loss that penalizes this.

The sparsity-prediction MLP is tiny, but on small datasets it can memorize token patterns instead of learning general routing logic. Gentle steer such as adding dropout (randomly zeroing weights during training to force the network to learn without relying on any single weight) or L2 weight penalty (adding a cost for large weights, discouraging overfitting) helps because they force the MLP to use only the most important patterns, blocking memorization.

If the sparsity loss weight is too high, lambda bounces wildly, and the router sends tokens to zero experts (no routing) or all experts (no sparsity). The paper tunes alpha and beta losses to balance this.

The paper uses three losses: language modeling loss (the real task), load-balancing loss (prevent collapse), and sparsity loss (steer toward target count). All three together keep the router stable and adaptive.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a tiny demo: a 3-layer MLP as the base model, 4 LoRA adapters, and LD-MoLE routing. Train it on a small classification task (for example, 2-class sentiment or MNIST digit). Measure the expert activation pattern (how many experts each token uses) as training progresses. Plot the per-token expert count over epochs. Show that early epochs show high variance (the MLP is learning), and by epoch 50, simple examples use 1-2 experts and complex examples use 3-4. Compare against fixed TopK (always 2 experts): LD-MoLE should reach the same or better accuracy on the training set and generalize better to a held-out test set, because it learned to allocate experts adaptively.
demo.metric_eq: test_accuracy_ld_mole minus test_accuracy_topk2 should be positive; mean_expert_count_per_token_by_class should show simple class lower than complex class
demo.closing: The demo is successful if test accuracy improves (showing the learned routing actually solves the task better), and if the plot shows the model learning to route simple tokens to fewer experts—visible proof that the learned adaptation is real and not just an artifact, because if routing were random or useless, the pattern would not emerge.
